hops.title: One receptor gene changes how a floral note smells
hops.text: Two people can sniff the same drink and describe it quite differently. Food makers add beta-ionone for a pleasant floral note, yet people differ enormously in how well they detect it. In 2013, researchers traced it to a single amino-acid change in one odorant receptor, OR5A1. The authors report that it explains over 96 percent of the observed variation, so sensitivity behaves almost like a single-gene trait. Sensitive people more easily tell which samples have added beta-ionone and often call it fragrant or floral, and the genotype also predicted different food and product choices. One receptor line reads the molecule differently, and what the person smells changes with it.

sources.citation: Jaeger SR et al., Curr Biol 23(16):1601-1605 (2013)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two roommates sniffing matching smoothies at a kitchen table, with small blossoms floating above one glass and plain air above the other.
image.caption: A one-amino-acid change in receptor OR5A1 shifts how strongly beta-ionone's floral note comes through.

hops.afterHeading: Sour and salt: the channel routes
hops.title: The champagne blues and the sour cells that taste fizz
hops.text: In 1988, two authors gave a strange drug side effect a memorable name: the champagne blues. Patients taking acetazolamide, which blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, reported that carbonated drinks tasted abnormal. That hinted carbonic anhydrase had a job in taste. Twenty-one years later, Charles Zuker's team silenced specific taste-cell classes in mice and found which cells use it. The sour-sensing cells are the taste sensors for carbonation, using carbonic anhydrase 4 to detect carbon dioxide. In mice lacking that enzyme, the taste nerve responded far less to carbon dioxide. A soda's tingle also comes from touch and irritation nerves, but its taste, in mice at least, runs through sour cells.

sources.citation: Graber M & Kelleher S, Am J Med 84(5):979-980 (1988); Kehrenberg MCA & Bachmann HS, Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol 395(6):619-627 (2022)

hops.afterHeading: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops
hops.title: Why a head cold makes food bland
hops.text: If you have had a bad head cold, you have probably noticed food go bland. Much of that loss is smell rather than taste: aromas from food in your mouth reach the nose from behind, by retronasal smell, and a cold weakens that route. When researchers in Dresden tested 58 people during an acute cold, their retronasal smell was reduced, and so was their sensitivity to salt. People blame their tongues anyway. In a University of Pennsylvania study of 750 smell-and-taste clinic patients, complaints of taste loss usually reflected a loss of smell, with upper respiratory infections among the top causes of lasting smell loss.

sources.citation: Deems DA et al., Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 117(5):519-528 (1991)
Pellegrino R et al., Int Forum Allergy Rhinol 7(2):185-191 (2017)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student in a scarf on a couch beside a tissue box, holding a steaming bowl of soup and looking puzzled.
image.caption: A cold weakens retronasal smell, which is why food seems bland while the tongue gets the blame.

audio.title: Sugar-blind cats, salty licorice and a chocolate trail
audio.transcript: Here are three true stories in which the wiring of smell and taste shows up in unexpected places. First, if you have ever watched a cat ignore a sweet treat, you may be seeing taste receptor genetics in action. Mammals normally build their sweet receptor by pairing two proteins, T one R two and T one R three. In two thousand five, researchers examined both genes in domestic cats. The cats had an apparently healthy T one R three gene, which they still need, paired with T one R one, for umami, the savory taste of meat. Their T one R two gene, though, was broken: it was missing two hundred forty-seven base pairs in exon three and carried early stop signals. When the team checked that damaged stretch in six more cats, a tiger and a cheetah, every one showed the same defects. Without T one R two, cats cannot assemble a working sweet receptor. Birds lack T one R two as well, which raised an awkward puzzle: how do hummingbirds taste sugary nectar? In two thousand fourteen, scientists found the answer. Since the hummingbird lineage split from insect-eating swifts, its version of the ancestral umami receptor, T one R one plus T one R three, has gained the ability to detect sugars. Birds lost one sweet receptor part, and hummingbirds later retuned another receptor to fill the gap. Second, consider Scandinavian salty licorice, a dark candy flavoured with ammonium chloride. Many newcomers find it aversive, while people raised on it can grow genuinely fond of it. For decades, neuroscientists used ammonium chloride as a standard control stimulus when recording from taste nerves, though how it activates taste cells was poorly understood. In two thousand twenty-three, Emily Liman's laboratory reported an unexpected answer: O top one, the same proton channel that type three cells use to taste sour acid. In lab-grown cells carrying mouse or human O top one, ammonium chloride raised the p H inside the cells, and current flowed in through the channel. Mice engineered without O top one lost most of their taste-cell and nerve responses to ammonium chloride. So the channel that helps mice taste acid also drives much of their taste-nerve response to the ingredient that gives salty licorice its bite. Third, a stubborn myth about your own nose. For more than a hundred years, people claimed humans have a poor sense of smell. That reputation traces back to the nineteenth-century anatomist Paul Broca, who based it on brain anatomy rather than on tests of human noses. He noticed that our olfactory bulb is small relative to our huge frontal lobes and guessed that human free will required a smaller role for smell. In absolute size, our olfactory bulb is actually quite large, with a comparable number of neurons to other mammals, and we even beat dogs and rodents on certain odors. To put human noses to the test, researchers laid a ten-meter trail of chocolate oil across a grassy field and asked thirty-two blindfolded volunteers to follow it. Twenty-one of the thirty-two, about two-thirds, tracked the trail by smell alone. Four volunteers who trained over a few days more than doubled their tracking speed. The researchers also found that the two nostrils sample air from spots about three and a half centimeters apart, and that having those two separate samples helps people follow a trail. Your nose is doing far more work than Broca ever gave it credit for.
